title: Ollama Introduction
readingMarkdown:
# Ollama Introduction

**Ollama** is the most popular way to run open-weight models on your own computer. In one tool it combines a **model runner**, built on llama.cpp-style inference for most models, a **registry** of ready-to-run models, a **command-line interface**, a **local HTTP API** that applications call, and, on macOS and Windows, a desktop app. Its documentation describes it as a way to use open models in desktop apps and coding agents, or build them into applications.

This module explains Ollama's architecture: the server, the CLI, the model library and naming, and the **Modelfile** that defines custom models. Later modules install it, Module 10.3; download models, Module 10.4; and connect applications, Module 10.11. Facts are as documented at the time of writing (November 2026); Ollama releases often, so check the docs for your version.

## 1. First-Principles Mental Model & Intuition

### A record player with a record shop next door

Think of Ollama as a record player with a record shop attached. The **record shop** is the model library: you ask for "qwen3:8b" and it fetches the right record. The **turntable** is the server, which loads a model into memory and plays it, generating text. The **buttons** are the CLI: play, fetch, list, stop. The **line-out socket** is the API, which lets other equipment, your applications, use the music. And a **Modelfile** is like a playlist card stuck to a record: "play this record, a bit quieter, with this introduction", a custom model built on a base.

```text
   ollama.com/library  (registry)            Hugging Face (hf.co/user/repo)  (GGUF repositories)
            \  pull                              /  pull
             v                                  v
   +--------------------- OLLAMA SERVER  127.0.0.1:11434 ----------------------+
   |  model store (~/.ollama/models)   loader: GPU / CPU / split   keep-alive  |
   |  inference engine (llama.cpp-style)        scheduler: parallel requests    |
   +----------------^------------------------------^----------------------------+
                    | HTTP: /api/chat, /api/generate, /api/embed, /v1/chat/completions (OpenAI-compatible)
        CLI: ollama run | pull | ls | ps | stop | rm | create | show | serve
        Desktop app (macOS, Windows)        Your applications (Module 10.11)
   Modelfile: FROM base + PARAMETER + SYSTEM + TEMPLATE + MESSAGE  ->  ollama create
```

### Why a server

Loading a model takes seconds and gigabytes of memory, so Ollama loads it once and keeps it ready for a while, serving every client, CLI, app, and script, from the same process. When nobody has used a model for a time, it is unloaded to free memory. Understanding this lifecycle explains most of Ollama's behaviour, including why the first request after a pause is slow.

## 2. Core Theory, Mathematical Foundations & Architecture Internals

### The server

The Ollama server listens by default on `127.0.0.1` port `11434`, as the FAQ states: only programs on the same machine can reach it. The API base is `http://localhost:11434/api`. Exposing it to a network by changing the bind address with `OLLAMA_HOST` is possible but means anyone who can reach the port can use your models, so it needs firewalling or a proxy with authentication, Module 10.13.

The server decides where each model runs: entirely on the GPU, entirely on the CPU, or **split** between them when it does not fit in GPU memory. A split model works but generates much more slowly, because layers on the CPU become the bottleneck. Models stay loaded for a **keep-alive** period, five minutes by default according to the FAQ, then unload.

### The CLI

The command-line interface, documented on the CLI page, covers the lifecycle:

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `ollama run <model>` | Download if needed, load, and chat; also accepts a one-off prompt |
| `ollama pull <model>` | Download a model |
| `ollama ls` | List downloaded models |
| `ollama ps` | List loaded models, with where they run and until when |
| `ollama stop <model>` | Unload a model now |
| `ollama rm <model>` | Delete a downloaded model |
| `ollama create <name> -f Modelfile` | Build a custom model |
| `ollama show --modelfile <model>` | Print a model's Modelfile |
| `ollama serve` | Run the server in the foreground; `ollama serve --help` lists its environment variables |

### Model names and tags

A model reference has a name and an optional **tag**, `name:tag`. Without a tag, Ollama uses `latest`, so `llama3.2` means `llama3.2:latest`. Library models live under a default namespace, so `qwen3:8b` is the official Qwen3 model with the `8b` tag; organisations can publish under their own namespace, `myteam/shop-assistant:v2`. Hugging Face documents running GGUF repositories directly with a reference such as `hf.co/{username}/{repository}:{quantization}`. Tags usually encode size and sometimes quantization; the tags page of each model on ollama.com lists what is available, Module 10.4.

Ollama also offers **cloud models**, run on Ollama's service rather than your hardware, with tags such as `:cloud` and an Ollama account. They are useful for trying larger models, but they are not local: data leaves your machine, which matters for the reasons you chose local in Module 10.1. The docs describe a setting to disable cloud features entirely.

### The Modelfile

A **Modelfile** defines a model as a base plus customisations. The reference lists instructions including:

| Instruction | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `FROM` | Required: the base, a model name, a GGUF file, or a Safetensors directory |
| `PARAMETER` | A runtime parameter such as `temperature`, `num_ctx`, `top_p`, `stop` |
| `SYSTEM` | The system prompt |
| `TEMPLATE` | The prompt template that formats messages for the model |
| `MESSAGE` | Example conversation turns |
| `LICENSE` | The licence text |
| `REQUIRES` | The minimum Ollama version |

Multi-line values use triple quotes, `"""`. Instructions are not case sensitive. `ollama create` builds the custom model; it reuses the base model's weights, so a customised model costs little extra disk space.

### Which parameters apply

A parameter can come from three places, applied in order, each overriding the previous:

$$\text{effective} = \text{defaults} \;\oplus\; \text{Modelfile PARAMETER} \;\oplus\; \text{request options}$$

The Modelfile reference documents defaults such as temperature 0.8, `top_k` 40, `top_p` 0.9, and repeat penalty 1.0. The **context length**, `num_ctx`, deserves care: Ollama's documentation has described different defaults in different places, and its context-length page describes a default that depends on available GPU memory, 4,096 tokens below 24 GiB, 32,768 tokens from 24 to 48 GiB, and 256K tokens at 48 GiB or more. A server-wide default can be set with `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH`. Because a too-short context silently truncates long prompts, Module 10.14, set `num_ctx` explicitly for any serious use.

### Keep-alive and cold starts

When a request arrives for a model that is not loaded, the server loads it first: a **cold start** of seconds to tens of seconds, depending on model size and disk speed. With keep-alive $k$ minutes, a request at time $t$ is warm if the previous request was at most $k$ minutes earlier. For a sequence of request times $t_1 < t_2 < \dots$:

$$\text{cold loads} = 1 + \left|\{\, i > 1 : t_i - t_{i-1} > k \,\}\right|$$

A longer keep-alive means fewer cold starts but memory held longer; a request can set `keep_alive` per call, and a negative value keeps a model loaded indefinitely, `0` unloads it immediately.

### Ollama compared with the alternatives

Module 10.1 introduced llama.cpp, LM Studio, and vLLM. Ollama's niche is **simplicity with an API**: one install, a curated registry, sensible defaults, a stable local HTTP API with OpenAI-compatible endpoints, and integrations with many tools. It gives up some control compared with raw llama.cpp, has no graphical model browser as rich as LM Studio's, and is not designed for high-concurrency production serving the way vLLM is.

### Complexity

Parsing a reference is linear in its length. Parsing a Modelfile is linear in lines. Merging parameters is linear in their number. Parsing `ollama ps` is linear in rows. Counting cold loads is linear in requests.

## 3. Production-Grade Implementation & Annotated Walkthrough

First, model references.

```python
import re

def parse_ref(ref):
    host, rest = None, ref
    if "/" in ref and "." in ref.split("/")[0]:
        host, rest = ref.split("/", 1)
    name, _, tag = rest.partition(":")
    namespace, _, model = name.rpartition("/")
    return {"host": host or "registry.ollama.ai", "namespace": namespace or "library", "model": model, "tag": tag or "latest"}

for ref in ["qwen3:8b", "llama3.2", "myteam/shop-assistant:v2", "hf.co/bartowski/Qwen3-8B-GGUF:Q4_K_M"]:
    print(ref, parse_ref(ref))
```

- **A first segment containing a dot is a host.** `hf.co` points at Hugging Face.
- **No namespace means the official library; no tag means `latest`.**
- **`llama3.2` is `llama3.2:latest`.** Pin explicit tags in applications so an update does not change the model underneath you.

Next, reading a Modelfile.

```python
INSTRUCTIONS = {"FROM", "PARAMETER", "TEMPLATE", "SYSTEM", "LICENSE", "MESSAGE", "REQUIRES"}

def parse_modelfile(text):
    mf = {"from": None, "parameters": {}, "system": None, "template": None, "messages": [], "errors": []}
    lines, i = text.splitlines(), 0
    while i < len(lines):
        line = lines[i].strip()
        i += 1
        if not line or line.startswith("#"):
            continue
        word, _, arg = line.partition(" ")
        word, arg = word.upper(), arg.strip()
        if arg.startswith('"""'):
            body = arg[3:]
            while '"""' not in body and i < len(lines):
                body += "\n" + lines[i]
                i += 1
            arg = body.split('"""')[0].strip()
        if word not in INSTRUCTIONS:
            mf["errors"].append(f"unknown instruction {word}")
            continue
        if word == "FROM":
            mf["from"] = arg
        elif word == "PARAMETER":
            key, _, value = arg.partition(" ")
            value = value.strip()
            try:
                value = int(value)
            except ValueError:
                try:
                    value = float(value)
                except ValueError:
                    value = value.strip('"')
            if key == "stop":
                mf["parameters"].setdefault("stop", []).append(value)
            else:
                mf["parameters"][key] = value
        elif word == "SYSTEM":
            mf["system"] = arg
        elif word == "TEMPLATE":
            mf["template"] = arg
        elif word == "MESSAGE":
            role, _, content = arg.partition(" ")
            mf["messages"].append((role, content))
    if not mf["from"]:
        mf["errors"].append("FROM is required")
    return mf

MODELFILE = '''# Tool shop assistant
FROM qwen3:8b
PARAMETER temperature 0.3
PARAMETER num_ctx 8192
PARAMETER stop "<|im_end|>"
SYSTEM """You are the tool shop's assistant.
Answer briefly and politely."""
MESSAGE user Do you sell SAW-3?
MESSAGE assistant Yes, SAW-3 is in stock.
'''
print(parse_modelfile(MODELFILE))
```

- **`FROM` names the base; it is required.**
- **Parameters are typed: integers, floats, or strings.** `stop` can appear several times, so it collects a list.
- **Triple-quoted values span lines.** The system prompt here is two lines.
- **Unknown instructions are reported.** A typo such as `SYSTM` would otherwise be silently ignored by a careless parser.

Then, the parameters that actually apply.

```python
DEFAULTS = {"temperature": 0.8, "top_k": 40, "top_p": 0.9, "repeat_penalty": 1.0}

def default_context(vram_gib):
    if vram_gib < 24:
        return 4096
    if vram_gib < 48:
        return 32768
    return 262144

def effective(modelfile_params, request_options, vram_gib, env_context=None):
    params = {**DEFAULTS, "num_ctx": env_context or default_context(vram_gib)}
    params.update(modelfile_params)
    params.update(request_options)
    return params

mf_params = parse_modelfile(MODELFILE)["parameters"]
print(effective(mf_params, {"temperature": 0.0}, vram_gib=12))
print(effective({}, {}, vram_gib=32)["num_ctx"], effective({}, {}, vram_gib=8, env_context=8192)["num_ctx"])
```

- **Defaults, then the Modelfile, then the request.** The request's temperature of 0 wins over the Modelfile's 0.3.
- **The Modelfile's `num_ctx` of 8,192 overrides the 12 GiB default of 4,096.**
- **Without a Modelfile value, the context follows GPU memory or the environment variable.**

Then, reading `ollama ps`.

```python
PS = """NAME          ID              SIZE      PROCESSOR          UNTIL
qwen3:8b      500a1f067a9f    6.5 GB    100% GPU           4 minutes from now
llama3:70b    bcfb190ca3a7    42 GB     48%/52% CPU/GPU    4 minutes from now
gemma4:4b     a2af6cc3eb7f    4.1 GB    100% CPU           Forever"""

def parse_ps(text):
    rows = []
    for line in text.strip().splitlines()[1:]:
        cols = re.split(r"\s{2,}", line.strip())
        name, size, processor = cols[0], cols[2], cols[3]
        split = re.match(r"(\d+)%/(\d+)% CPU/GPU", processor)
        if split:
            cpu, gpu = int(split.group(1)), int(split.group(2))
        elif processor.endswith("GPU"):
            cpu, gpu = 0, int(processor.split("%")[0])
        else:
            cpu, gpu = int(processor.split("%")[0]), 0
        verdict = "fully on GPU" if gpu == 100 else ("CPU only" if gpu == 0 else "split: expect slower generation")
        rows.append((name, size, cpu, gpu, verdict))
    return rows

for row in parse_ps(PS):
    print(row)
```

- **Columns are separated by two or more spaces.**
- **`100% GPU` is the fast case.** The documentation describes this column as the way to check GPU use.
- **`48%/52% CPU/GPU` means the 70B model did not fit; generation will be much slower.**
- **`100% CPU` on a machine with a GPU means the GPU was not used,** a troubleshooting signal, Module 10.14.

Finally, keep-alive and cold starts.

```python
def cold_loads(request_minutes, keep_alive_minutes=5):
    loads, loaded_until = 0, None
    for t in request_minutes:
        if loaded_until is None or t > loaded_until:
            loads += 1
        loaded_until = t + keep_alive_minutes
    return loads

REQUESTS = [0, 2, 4, 12, 13, 30, 31, 60]
print(cold_loads(REQUESTS), cold_loads(REQUESTS, 30), cold_loads(REQUESTS, 0))
```

- **With the default five minutes, gaps of 8, 17, and 29 minutes each cause a reload: 4 cold loads.**
- **With 30 minutes, the model stays warm all hour: 1 load, at the cost of memory held longer.**
- **With 0, every request reloads: 8.** Useful only when memory is very tight.

**Complexity.** `parse_ref` is linear in the reference. `parse_modelfile` is linear in lines. `effective` merges small dictionaries. `parse_ps` and `cold_loads` are linear in rows and requests.

### An Ollama setup note for the tool shop

```text
SERVER       default 127.0.0.1:11434, local only; OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH not set (Modelfile sets num_ctx)
MODELS       qwen3:8b (pinned tag), built into shop-assistant via Modelfile
MODELFILE    FROM qwen3:8b; temperature 0.3; num_ctx 8192; SYSTEM prompt; two example MESSAGE turns
KEEP-ALIVE   30 minutes during opening hours (requests every few minutes); default overnight
CHECKS       ollama ps shows 100% GPU after first request; ollama show --modelfile shop-assistant reviewed
CLOUD        cloud models disabled: customer data must stay local
```

## 4. Practitioner Wisdom & Edge Cases (Reddit / HN / Stack Overflow Synthesis)

**Untagged references in applications.** `latest` can change. Pin tags.

**Assuming defaults.** Context length defaults have differed between versions and hardware. Set `num_ctx`.

**Typos in Modelfiles.** An unrecognised instruction can be silently missed. Check with `ollama show --modelfile`.

**Long system prompts, short context.** The system prompt plus history must fit. Size `num_ctx` accordingly.

**Slow first request.** That is a cold start. Raise keep-alive or preload the model.

**Models stuck in memory.** A long keep-alive holds gigabytes. Use `ollama stop` or a shorter keep-alive.

**Split CPU/GPU without noticing.** Generation slows dramatically. Check `ollama ps`.

**Exposing the server to the network.** Anyone who can reach the port can use it. Keep the default or protect it.

**Cloud tags on a privacy-sensitive task.** `:cloud` models run elsewhere. Check the tag; disable cloud features if needed.

**Wrong prompt template for imported GGUF files.** Chat formatting breaks. Use the model's template, Module 10.14.

**Mixing stop sequences.** Several `stop` parameters accumulate. Review the effective list.

**Forgetting Ollama updates.** Fixes and new model support arrive often. Update regularly, and re-test.

## 5. Active Recall Check & Synthesis Summary

**Summary.** Ollama combines a local server, by default on 127.0.0.1 port 11434, a model registry, a CLI, a local HTTP API with OpenAI-compatible endpoints, and desktop apps on macOS and Windows. The server loads models onto the GPU, CPU, or both, keeps them loaded for a keep-alive period, five minutes by default, and unloads them afterwards, so requests after longer gaps start cold. CLI commands run, pull, list, inspect, stop, remove, and create models. References take the form name:tag, defaulting to latest and the official library, with Hugging Face GGUF repositories reachable by host prefix, and cloud-tagged models running off the machine. A Modelfile builds a custom model from a required FROM base with PARAMETER, SYSTEM, TEMPLATE, MESSAGE, LICENSE, and REQUIRES instructions. Effective parameters layer defaults, Modelfile values, and request options, and the context length should be set explicitly. `ollama ps` shows whether a model runs fully on the GPU, on the CPU, or split. Ollama's niche is simplicity with an API, compared with llama.cpp's control, LM Studio's graphical interface, and vLLM's serving throughput.

**Question 1.** A developer's application calls `llama3.2` and works for months, then its answers change style overnight. Using `parse_ref`, explain what probably happened and how to prevent it.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

`parse_ref("llama3.2")` shows the reference resolves to the official library model with the tag `latest`, because no tag was given. `latest` is a moving pointer: when the model publisher or the registry updates what `latest` points to, a later `ollama pull`, or an automated update, fetches a different model under the same name, and the application silently starts using it. The change in style is a different model, or a different version or quantization, not a bug in the application. To prevent it, pin an explicit tag that identifies size and, where available, quantization, in the application's configuration; better still, build a custom model with a Modelfile whose `FROM` names the pinned tag, giving the application a stable name such as `shop-assistant` that the team controls; and treat model upgrades like any other release: pull the new version deliberately, run the evaluation set, Module 8.12 and Module 10.15, and switch only when it passes.

</details>

**Question 2.** The shop's Modelfile sets `num_ctx 8192` and `temperature 0.3`, and a request sends `temperature 0`. The server runs on a 12 GiB GPU. Use `effective` to state the parameters that apply, and explain why setting `num_ctx` explicitly matters.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

`effective` starts from the defaults, temperature 0.8, top_k 40, top_p 0.9, repeat penalty 1.0, and a context of 4,096 because the GPU has under 24 GiB; applies the Modelfile, temperature 0.3, num_ctx 8,192, and its stop sequence; then applies the request, temperature 0. The result is temperature 0, num_ctx 8,192, top_k 40, top_p 0.9, repeat penalty 1.0, and the stop list. Setting `num_ctx` explicitly matters because the default is not stable: Ollama's own documentation has described different defaults in different places and, on its context-length page, a default that depends on available GPU memory, so the same application could get 4,096 tokens on one machine and 32,768 on another. When a prompt is longer than the context, the beginning is cut off without an error, so a long system prompt or document can silently disappear, producing confusing answers, Module 10.14. An explicit value, sized for the system prompt, conversation history, and expected documents, and checked against memory, Module 10.10, makes behaviour predictable everywhere.

</details>

**Question 3.** Staff complain that the assistant takes 20 seconds to answer the first question after lunch but is quick afterwards. Using `cold_loads` and `parse_ps`, explain the behaviour and propose a fix.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

The model unloads after its keep-alive period, five minutes by default, so the first request after a longer gap triggers a cold start: the server reads gigabytes of weights from disk into GPU memory before generating anything, which can take seconds to tens of seconds. `cold_loads` shows the pattern: with requests at minutes 0, 2, 4, 12, 13, 30, 31, and 60 and a five-minute keep-alive, the gaps of 8, 17, and 29 minutes each cause a reload, four cold starts in an hour, while a 30-minute keep-alive needs only one. After lunch the gap is long, so the first request is always cold. Fixes: set a longer keep-alive during opening hours, through the `OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE` environment variable or a `keep_alive` value on requests, accepting that the model holds memory longer; or preload the model with a scheduled request at the start of the afternoon. `parse_ps` should also be checked: if the model shows `100% CPU` or a CPU/GPU split, every request is slow, not just the first, and the fix is a smaller model or quantization that fits the GPU, Module 10.10.

</details>

The instruction is the first word in upper case and the argument the rest; an argument starting with three double quotes continues over following lines until the closing triple quote, and its inner text is stripped. Record 'unknown instruction <WORD>' for instructions not in INSTRUCTIONS. FROM, SYSTEM, and TEMPLATE set their fields; PARAMETER splits key and value and converts the value to int, else float, else a string with double quotes stripped, collecting repeated 'stop' values in a list; MESSAGE appends (role, content). Add 'FROM is required' if there is no FROM. Parse the shop's Modelfile and a faulty one. This is the Modelfile from Section 2. [MOD-10.2]
steps.hintConceptual: Read the playlist card line by line: which record to play, how to set the controls, what to say first, and flag any line you do not recognise.
steps.testAssertion:
_m = parse_modelfile(MODELFILE)
assert _m is not None and _m["from"] == "qwen3:8b" and _m["parameters"] == {"temperature": 0.3, "num_ctx": 8192, "stop": ["<|im_end|>"]}, f"Base and typed parameters, got {_m}"
assert _m["system"] == "You are the tool shop's assistant.\nAnswer briefly and politely." and _m["messages"] == [("user", "Do you sell SAW-3?"), ("assistant", "Yes, SAW-3 is in stock.")] and _m["errors"] == [], "Multi-line system prompt and messages"
assert parse_modelfile("parameter temperature 1\nSYSTM hi")["errors"] == ["unknown instruction SYSTM", "FROM is required"], "Typos and missing FROM"
assert parse_modelfile('from x\nPARAMETER stop "a"\nPARAMETER stop "b"')["parameters"]["stop"] == ["a", "b"], "Case-insensitive; stop accumulates"
print("Step 2 passed: base qwen3:8b, three parameters, a two-line system prompt, two example turns.")

steps.title: Work out effective parameters
steps.instruction: Implement default_context(vram_gib): 4096 below 24, 32768 below 48, otherwise 262144. Implement effective(modelfile_params, request_options, vram_gib, env_context): start from DEFAULTS plus num_ctx set to env_context or default_context(vram_gib), then apply the Modelfile parameters, then the request options. Work out the parameters for three situations and check four context tiers. This is which parameters apply from Section 2. [MOD-10.2]
steps.hintConceptual: Factory settings, then the settings written on the playlist card, then whatever the listener asks for right now; the last word wins.
steps.testAssertion:
_mp = {"temperature": 0.3, "num_ctx": 8192, "stop": ["<|im_end|>"]}
assert effective(_mp, {"temperature": 0.0}, 12) == {"temperature": 0.0, "top_k": 40, "top_p": 0.9, "repeat_penalty": 1.0, "num_ctx": 8192, "stop": ["<|im_end|>"]}, f"Request beats Modelfile beats defaults, got {effective(_mp, {'temperature': 0.0}, 12)}"
assert [default_context(12), default_context(24), default_context(47.9), default_context(48)] == [4096, 32768, 32768, 262144], "VRAM tiers"
assert effective({}, {}, 32)["num_ctx"] == 32768 and effective({}, {}, 8, env_context=8192)["num_ctx"] == 8192, "Environment variable"
print("Step 3 passed: temperature 0 from the request, 8,192 context from the Modelfile.")

steps.title: Read ollama ps
steps.instruction: Implement parse_ps(text). Skip the header line; split each row on runs of two or more spaces, taking the name, size, and processor from columns 0, 2, and 3. Parse the processor: 'a%/b% CPU/GPU' gives cpu a and gpu b; 'n% GPU' gives 0 and n; 'n% CPU' gives n and 0. The verdict is 'fully on GPU' when gpu is 100, 'CPU only' when it is 0, otherwise 'split: expect slower generation'. Return (name, size, cpu, gpu, verdict) per row. Read the three loaded models. This is the server from Section 2. [MOD-10.2]
steps.hintConceptual: The status board says which records are on the fast turntable, which on the slow one, and which are awkwardly balanced across both.
steps.hintSyntax:
rows = []
for line in text.strip().splitlines()[1:]:
    cols = re.split(r"\s{2,}", line.strip())
    name, size, processor = cols[0], cols[2], cols[3]
    split = re.match(r"(\d+)%/(\d+)% CPU/GPU", processor)
    if split: cpu, gpu = int(split.group(1)), int(split.group(2))
    elif processor.endswith("GPU"): cpu, gpu = 0, int(processor.split("%")[0])
    else: cpu, gpu = int(processor.split("%")[0]), 0
    verdict = "fully on GPU" if gpu == 100 else ("CPU only" if gpu == 0 else "split: expect slower generation")
    rows.append((name, size, cpu, gpu, verdict))
return rows
steps.testAssertion:
_ps = parse_ps(PS)
assert _ps == [("qwen3:8b", "6.5 GB", 0, 100, "fully on GPU"), ("llama3:70b", "42 GB", 48, 52, "split: expect slower generation"), ("gemma4:4b", "4.1 GB", 100, 0, "CPU only")], f"Three rows, got {_ps}"
assert parse_ps("NAME  ID  SIZE  PROCESSOR  UNTIL") == [], "Header only"
print("Step 4 passed: the 70B model is split 48/52 between CPU and GPU.")

steps.title: Count cold starts
steps.instruction: Implement cold_loads(request_minutes, keep_alive_minutes). Go through the request times in order; count a cold load when nothing is loaded yet or the time is after loaded_until; after each request set loaded_until to its time plus the keep-alive. Count cold loads for the morning's requests with keep-alives of 5, 30, and 0 minutes. This is keep-alive and cold starts from Section 2. [MOD-10.2]
steps.hintConceptual: Every time the record has been put away because nobody asked for a while, the next listener waits while it is fetched and put back on.
steps.testAssertion:
assert cold_loads(REQUESTS) == 4 and cold_loads(REQUESTS, 30) == 1 and cold_loads(REQUESTS, 0) == 8, f"Keep-alive changes cold starts, got {[cold_loads(REQUESTS), cold_loads(REQUESTS, 30), cold_loads(REQUESTS, 0)]}"
assert cold_loads([]) == 0 and cold_loads([0, 5, 10]) == 1 and cold_loads([0, 6]) == 2, "Boundaries: exactly at the limit stays warm"
print("Step 5 passed: four cold starts an hour at the default, one with 30 minutes.")
